utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please be seated. Have the accused brought in, please, Mr. Registrar. (The accused entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Good morning to the interpreters and to Defence and Prosecution counsel, to the accused. We will resume our work now, once the witness, Father Pervan, has come into the courtroom. It's Father Ivan Pervan; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: But the family name is Pervan.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Ivan Pervan, that's correct, yes. (The witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Father Ivan, do you feel all right? Did you rest well last night? We can resume our work. Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Yes, I can hear you very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Cayley?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours, good morning counsel. Good morning, Mr. Pervan.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. Pervan, yesterday you stated that Father Bozo was an honest man who very often criticised the authorities in Kiseljak for the difficulties that the Muslims were having to undergo; do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: FATHER IVAN PERVAN
utterances.text: Yes, Father Bozo very often in our meetings spoke about errors, that is to say the difficulties that the Muslims had to pass through. Those same difficulties that they had to go through is something that I spoke about publicly. Bozo was not in Kiseljak. He was in Lepenica. That was where his duties were, and at that time, it was necessary to speak of these problems that these people encountered.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Who did he address within the HVO authorities in Kiseljak about?

utterances.speaker: FATHER IVAN PERVAN
utterances.text: I do not know that he addressed them officially, because he saw them very rarely, but as Kiseljak is not a large town, he was able to meet them. He was able to see them, for example, when he asked permission for the office in which he was located. So, I don't know that he did publicly address them or wrote to them. Whether he telephoned them, I cannot say.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I would be right to say that he spoke to Mr. Josip Boro and Mr. Ivica Rajic, Mr. Miro Bozic about the problems, the difficulties that the Muslims were suffering in Kiseljak?

utterances.speaker: FATHER IVAN PERVAN
utterances.text: I cannot confirm that because I don't know about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: You don't know who he spoke to within the HVO authorities in Kiseljak about the difficulties of the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: FATHER IVAN PERVAN
utterances.text: No, I don't know who he spoke to, but he felt this, and he had the need to speak to us clergymen at our meetings and when we would meet. So, I don't know who he spoke about this to. He did have a need to speak about it, but I don't know who he actually spoke to.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, let's speak about the meaning of the word "difficulties." Now, I'm right in saying, am I not, that difficulties means the looting of Muslim property, the torching of their homes, and the forced expulsion of Muslims from Kiseljak; that's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: FATHER IVAN PERVAN
utterances.text: Yes, you're right, those are difficulties for everyone to whom such a difficulty occurs.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, you said yesterday, and you said again today that you made criticism from the altar of your church about the suffering of the Muslim community in Kiseljak. Did you name any individuals that were involved in creating these difficulties for the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: FATHER IVAN PERVAN
utterances.text: On several occasions I did speak about the evils that were taking place in our area. I was not present when the difficulties happened, that is to say, I don't know who destroyed and set fire to the Merhamet. I don't know which group of people did that, and I did not decisively name anybody from the altar, from the pulpit, and it is not the practice of the church to condemn any individual human being from the altar.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, you said yesterday that you were aware that fighting took place in Rotilj in April of 1993; is that right?

utterances.speaker: FATHER IVAN PERVAN
utterances.text: Yes, when I came back from Split I learned of the fighting that had gone on up there, that there were dead, and that there were facilities which were set fire to. I learned of this from the people when I returned to Kiseljak.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Are you aware, Mr. Pervan, that the HVO commenced combat operations on the 18th of April, 1993, in the Kiseljak municipality?

utterances.speaker: FATHER IVAN PERVAN
utterances.text: The fighting took place on the one side between the national communities, ethnic groups, that is to say, the Croats and Muslims or the Muslims and Croats, and quite obviously at that time and already in 1992 the HVO had been formed and the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina had been set up. So, I think that the war was a war between two armies.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Have you seen any written combat orders prior to your testimony today?

utterances.speaker: FATHER IVAN PERVAN
utterances.text: I have not seen any written combat orders. I didn't see any then or since then, now or at any time.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Well, if the witness could be shown Exhibit 456/22, please. That's Prosecutor's Exhibit 456/22. If, Mr. Registrar, you could have Defence Exhibit 306, Prosecutor's Exhibit 456/50 and Prosecutor's Exhibit 298 handy, that would be useful.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, Father, I know you're not a military man, but I would like to draw your attention to a number of points in this order. You will see that the date of the order is the 17th of April, 1993; do you see that?

utterances.speaker: FATHER IVAN PERVAN
utterances.text: I apologise, but I was busy reading through the document and I didn't realise that you were addressing me. Could you please repeat the question and just give me a few moments to read the document?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. Pervan, just read through the document and then I will ask you the question.

utterances.speaker: FATHER IVAN PERVAN
utterances.text: Very well, thank you. Yes, I've read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, you would agree with me that this order was issued on the 17th of April; wouldn't you, 1993?

utterances.speaker: FATHER IVAN PERVAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Quite simply, it's an order for combat operations; is it not?

utterances.speaker: FATHER IVAN PERVAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: In paragraph 2, the assignment for the Ban Jelacic Brigade is set out, and I will summarise it; essentially to capture the villages of Gomionica and Svinjarevo through the systematic use of various types of mortar. Do you agree with me there?

utterances.speaker: FATHER IVAN PERVAN
utterances.text: That's what it says.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: The operation is to begin on the 18th of April, 1993, at 0530 hours? That's in paragraph 10.

utterances.speaker: FATHER IVAN PERVAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: The order is, in fact, signed by Tihomir Blaskic.

utterances.speaker: FATHER IVAN PERVAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If the witness could now be shown Exhibit D306.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Have you read it?

utterances.speaker: FATHER IVAN PERVAN
utterances.text: Yes, I have, I have read it. I have not read everything, because some of the things are illegible, like the title at the top of the page, the heading.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I can assist you there. The date is, in fact, the 18th of April, 1993, and the time is 1645 hours. You would agree with me that this is a report in response to the order that I've just read out to you of the 17th of April? This is a response from the Ban Jelacic Brigade to the Central Bosnian Operative Zone; is it not?

utterances.speaker: FATHER IVAN PERVAN
utterances.text: That's what it says, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: To summarise the report, it indicates that the conflict has spread to the villages of Rotilj, Visnjica, Dolce, Hercezi, and Brestoska?

utterances.speaker: FATHER IVAN PERVAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: It indicates that the HVO has not yet managed to take the village of Gomionica?

utterances.speaker: FATHER IVAN PERVAN
utterances.text: Well, if you're expecting an answer, then this is what I have to say: When I learned that I would come before this Honourable Trial Chamber one-and-a-half months ago, I talked to a man in Rotilj who was with a man in Borina who was there when the fighting took place in Rotilj. He told me that they did have an order at 0530 hours, but that they discussed this and that they wanted to surrender their arms. Having mentioned Gomionica, I said in my testimony yesterday that on the 7th I returned from Split via Fojnica and I was not able to pass at the Fojnica cross-roads, junction, because from the direction of Gomionica, which was not far from the road, there was constant shooting. I think that is an answer to what you have just asked me.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: The man that you discussed matters with in Rotilj, he was a member of the local HVO --

utterances.speaker: FATHER IVAN PERVAN
utterances.text: I apologise, Your Honour, I said the man from Borina and he was there when the fighting was going on in Rotilj. The man is from Borina.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: This gentleman from Borina who received this order to commence operations at 0530, he was a member of the HVO, wasn't he, at the time?

utterances.speaker: FATHER IVAN PERVAN
utterances.text: That man who told me about this a month-and-a-half ago was a member of the HVO, but he did not get an order. He just said, and I quote, that "The fighting was to have begun at 0530 hours. We stopped and continued negotiations."

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If the witness could be shown Exhibit 456/50, please.

utterances.speaker: FATHER IVAN PERVAN
utterances.text: I have read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: To summarise, this is an order of the 19th of April of 1993 to the Ban Jelacic Brigade from Colonel Blaskic urging the forces in Kiseljak to go on and take Gomionica; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FATHER IVAN PERVAN
utterances.text: That's what it says.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, if Exhibit 298 could be placed on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: This is in English, Mr. Pervan, so you won't need to read it, but I will read it out to you and counsel can follow along. Now, you would agree with me that those orders and reports, read together, show that a combat operation commenced on the 18th of April at 0530 in the morning and continued through in the 19th of April; would you agree with me there?

utterances.speaker: FATHER IVAN PERVAN
utterances.text: I would agree with you, with your sentence, but I should like to add that what I heard was that on the other side there were military units. That's what I heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, this next document is an ECMM report. You recall the ECMM in Kiseljak; do you not?

utterances.speaker: FATHER IVAN PERVAN
utterances.text: I do not at the moment recall any names, because there were so many people from monitoring missions, UNPROFOR and other people who were there doing I don't know what duty, passed through Kiseljak and through my own house, that it was a mass of people. But I did see people who were equipped, and whether they were wearing UNPROFOR uniforms or monitor uniforms, or whatever, but there were different groups of people there at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: But you recall the organisation of ECMM being present in Kiseljak in 1993.

utterances.speaker: FATHER IVAN PERVAN
utterances.text: Yes, there were monitors in Kiseljak.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: This is a report written by a witness who has given evidence before these Judges. It is dated the 25th of April, 1993, and it is titled "Special Report on Alleged Ethnic Cleansing." "From 1500 hours, 18th April, to 1200 hours 19 April, about 20 masked soldiers, alleged to be HVO, some possibly from the neighbourhood, kind of death commando, entered the above village and destroyed all the Muslim houses from the west part of the village. Nineteen houses, some garages, stables, and other constructions. The village was not defended by any force, since all of their soldiers were deployed in the Visoko area. None of the Croat houses were damaged. All of the houses were burned down, looted and some were vandalised. As this was happening, most of the inhabitants had been evacuated to the south-east older part, except for seven persons who were savagely executed. On the next morning many young and old men were arrested and put into gaol in the Kiseljak HVO prison." Now, Father, I know you were not there at the time, but is that what you heard happened in Rotilj on the 18th and 19th of April, 1993?

utterances.speaker: FATHER IVAN PERVAN
utterances.text: I did not hear about it in detail, so exhaustively.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Did you hear that Muslim houses had been looted and burned in Rotilj on the 18th and 19th of April, 1993?

utterances.speaker: FATHER IVAN PERVAN
utterances.text: Until the present day one can see that some houses are burned down and destroyed. I imagine that it is certain that there was looting and violent behaviour too.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Were any Croat houses looted and burned on that day in Rotilj?

utterances.speaker: FATHER IVAN PERVAN
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Are you aware of the murder of seven civilians in that village on the 18th of April?

utterances.speaker: FATHER IVAN PERVAN
utterances.text: I heard about that, notably the murder of a woman.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Zibija Skrso, does that name refresh your memory? Skrso? Perhaps it's my pronunciation.

utterances.speaker: FATHER IVAN PERVAN
utterances.text: I think that could be the name.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Let me read to you the list of people murdered that day and you can tell me whether or not you recognise them. "Zibija Skrso, a 31-year-old woman, raped and then killed by firearms. We saw the evidence in the house and the blood stains." Do you recall hearing that that had happened?

utterances.speaker: FATHER IVAN PERVAN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, as I was inquiring of the dead, I talked to a lady doctor who was in Rotilj, and she confirmed this. They called her to tell her that this woman was killed. She walked in and said the following. She said to me, "I walked in and I saw her with her head back, half sitting, half lying, and she had clothes on." I asked the lady doctor a few times, "Doctor, was she raped"? She said, "I cannot confirm that, all of this happened very quickly, and she was dressed, she had her clothes on." So I asked Dr. Golubovic this same question several times.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Do you recall that Miralem Topalovic and Esad Topalovic were both killed, father and son?

utterances.speaker: FATHER IVAN PERVAN
utterances.text: I must say the following, that in Kiseljak, when the fighting broke out, I had been the parish priest for only a year and a half. I didn't even know all my own parishioners and, especially, I didn't know all the Muslims, because they don't come to church anyway. I would see them seldom. I saw only a few people who held public posts in the municipality. I knew the people from Merhamet. I knew the hodzas, the Muslim clergymen, and their names. Someone such as Skrso, Pavlovic, Pusculovic, I'm aware of those family names, that those are family names from Kiseljak. I didn't know any one of these people, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So you didn't know Bajro Pusculovic and Zila Pusculovic?

utterances.speaker: FATHER IVAN PERVAN
utterances.text: No, I did not. Even now, I only know ten or fifteen Muslims by their names. I don't know their names and surnames. I don't even know all my own parishioners because, including the refugees, I have over 7.000 parishioners now, and it is quite difficult for anyone. I don't know all their names, surnames, and I don't know their faces, and I don't know their appearances.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Did you hear, after the event, of an elderly couple who had been burned alive in their house?

utterances.speaker: FATHER IVAN PERVAN
utterances.text: I think that this was being talked about.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Well, that was Mr. and Mrs. Pusculovic. I take it that you know nothing about the killing of Dzevad Hodzic and Jihad Kosavac?

utterances.speaker: FATHER IVAN PERVAN
utterances.text: I must tell you that I heard that there were people who were killed, who were dead, but no where did I see this list, so I cannot remember any individual murders. It is the first time on this screen that I see a list of people who got killed in Rotilj, if that is the list.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I'll move on, Mr. Pervan. If the usher could turn to the last page, I'll read the final paragraph, which reads as follows, and this was the finding of ECMM on 25 April, '93: "There are about 600 inhabitants that lived in the south-west part of the village. They are restricted to their village, being surrounded by HVO. They are without electricity, telephone, water supply, and food supply is low. They have an urgent need of a doctor or nurse. They have kids with high fever and no medication. Within this number, there are about 100 to 150 refugees from Visoko." When you returned in May, is that the position that you found in Rotilj?

utterances.speaker: FATHER IVAN PERVAN
utterances.text: I certainly did not go to Rotilj the very first day. I do not know what the situation was like during those days. I have said, and I state this with full responsibility, that there was a lady doctor in the village who certainly did stand by her doctor's oath and who certainly did favours to them. The military conflict and the shooting took their toll. People were frightened. We were all frightened. There were certainly dead people on both sides. There was fear. I know that houses and stables were burned down. As houses fell, the electricity lines and the telephone lines broke down in Kiseljak and in Rotilj, because these were transmission lines in the air. They were not in the ground. So this is quite plausible.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Your testimony is that, since you were not in Kiseljak on the 25th of April, 1993, you have no idea of the condition of the Muslim villages at that time; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FATHER IVAN PERVAN
utterances.text: Yes. I was not aware of this situation. I was in Split, and I did not have any telephone links with Kiseljak.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Father, are you aware of any investigation taking place by the civilian or military police into the events that occurred in Rotilj?

utterances.speaker: FATHER IVAN PERVAN
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Are you aware of anybody being punished for what happened in the village of Rotilj on the 18th and 19th of April, 1993?

utterances.speaker: FATHER IVAN PERVAN
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you. I've finished with that exhibit now.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Father, I want to explore with you the condition of the village of Rotilj and the Muslims living within it over the year of 1993. I don't want to go through every month, because we'll be here for weeks. What I wish to do with you is take three points in time where you can explain to the Judges what you found in the village of Rotilj. Have you taken a look at this aerial photograph that's on the easel?

utterances.speaker: FATHER IVAN PERVAN
utterances.text: Yes. I saw it yesterday when you put it up.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Did you recognise the area? I know you're a local, but it's not always easy to recognise one's place of residence from the air. Do you recognise it?

utterances.speaker: FATHER IVAN PERVAN
utterances.text: I would have to take a look from the front.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Please do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please come closer to the map. Get up and get closer to the map. The usher might help you with the microphone in order to help you answer more easily.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: If you allow, this is document 76.

utterances.speaker: FATHER IVAN PERVAN
utterances.text: Yes. I recognised it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Please remain standing. Could the usher please give Father Pervan a pointer?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Nobilo, you can approach the map as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. Pervan, can you point to the village of Borina on the map?

utterances.speaker: FATHER IVAN PERVAN
utterances.text: This is Donja Borina. This is Gornja Borina, a few houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: You are pointing to the houses which, on the photograph, are directly above the village of Rotilj. In fact, the road through Borina runs parallel to the road through Rotilj? Is that correct, what I've just said?

utterances.speaker: FATHER IVAN PERVAN
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: The village of Borina is, in fact, a Bosnian Croat village, is it not?

utterances.speaker: FATHER IVAN PERVAN
utterances.text: The village of Borina is a Croatian village.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: How far, in terms of distance, is Borina from Rotilj at the closest point?

utterances.speaker: FATHER IVAN PERVAN
utterances.text: The closest point is up here at the top of the village of Borina (indicating), and here is also a Croat house, so up here (indicating). Up here, I think these are Croat houses over here, and these are Muslim houses over here (indicating).

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: What would you estimate the distance to be in metres at the closest point between Rotilj and Borina?

utterances.speaker: FATHER IVAN PERVAN
utterances.text: From 10 to 100 metres. That is what I said yesterday. It's over here (indicating), and over here (indicating), the maximum is 300 metres, not even that much.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: On that side, the village of Borina runs parallel for the whole distance of the village of Rotilj; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FATHER IVAN PERVAN
utterances.text: Could you please repeat your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Am I right in saying that the village of Borina runs parallel and above the whole of the distance of the village of Rotilj?

utterances.speaker: FATHER IVAN PERVAN
utterances.text: Yes. Those are two parallel villages, two parallel villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: During the conflict, the HVO controlled the village of Borina, did it not?

utterances.speaker: FATHER IVAN PERVAN
utterances.text: Yes, it did.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: The Kiseljak barracks, how far are the Kiseljak barracks from Rotilj?

utterances.speaker: FATHER IVAN PERVAN
utterances.text: Five to seven minutes on foot.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: The village of Rotilj extends down a long road. What is the distance from the main road to the end of the village, approximately?

utterances.speaker: FATHER IVAN PERVAN
utterances.text: You mean from this point (indicating) to Kiseljak?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: FATHER IVAN PERVAN
utterances.text: I think two and a half kilometres. I never watched the clock in my car, but I think it's about four minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: An estimate is fine, Mr. Pervan. You're doing very well. The village of Rotilj is located --

utterances.speaker: FATHER IVAN PERVAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: -- the village of Rotilj is located in a valley, is it not --

utterances.speaker: FATHER IVAN PERVAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: -- with steep hills on both sides?

utterances.speaker: FATHER IVAN PERVAN
utterances.text: Well, not exactly. From Borina, yes, but towards Pazavici, there's a gentle slope.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: They will not be on this photograph, I suspect, but where was the confrontation line between the HVO and the ABiH. Where was the front-line?

utterances.speaker: FATHER IVAN PERVAN
utterances.text: I was not in Rotilj, and I don't know where this was. I can't answer that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: You don't know where the front-line was between the HVO and the ABiH?

utterances.speaker: FATHER IVAN PERVAN
utterances.text: That, I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I'll ask the question again. Subsequent to the 18th of April, 1993, were you aware where the front-line was between the HVO and the ABiH?

utterances.speaker: FATHER IVAN PERVAN
utterances.text: I simply don't understand your question. Are you asking me about Rotilj or are you asking me about whatever? I mean, after the 18th, in Rotilj -- I mean, I don't understand your question. You have to put it very accurately.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I'll give you a specific month. In November of 1993, are you aware where the front-line existed geographically, the front-line between the HVO and the ABiH?

utterances.speaker: FATHER IVAN PERVAN
utterances.text: In November, I do know where the front-line was between the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the Croatian Defence Council, but that line was far away from Rotilj, a few kilometres away from Rotilj. In 1993, at that time in Rotilj, there was not a front-line at all, nor in Borina. The front-lines were towards Visoko, towards Sarajevo, above Kresevo, behind Lug and near Brestovsko.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So the front-line is not on this photograph?

utterances.speaker: FATHER IVAN PERVAN
utterances.text: After the conflict in April, there was no front-line here anymore. There was no military there which would attack Rotilj. There were no lines in Borina. People lived in their houses normally, and the front-lines were a few kilometres away from Borina at Rotilj.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: They had moved east towards Visoko, hadn't they, the front-lines?

utterances.speaker: FATHER IVAN PERVAN
utterances.text: The front-line was within the borders of the Kiseljak municipality, except for that part of the municipality which was taken by the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, that is Kazagici, Gunjace, Datici, Bilalovac, and Badnja, towards Fojnica, behind Lug, and in Bakovici, towards Visoko, at Cikulja, and in Zavrsge, then further on towards Visoko after Celukovac. At Kobiljaca, the line was against the army of Republika Srpska, and in Lepenica and Belakovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Sir, in November of 1993, all of the area on this photograph was territory controlled by the HVO, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: FATHER IVAN PERVAN
utterances.text: Yes. It was under the control of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You can take your seat.

utterances.speaker: FATHER IVAN PERVAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, if you recall, and I apologise to Mr. Nobilo because I probably have to ask you to get up any second, but where were the Muslims located in the village of Rotilj, which part?

utterances.speaker: FATHER IVAN PERVAN
utterances.text: The Muslims were in this part of the village here. That was a Muslim house. These houses were Muslim. This was a Croat house. These are Muslim houses, and so were these, these too. This was a Croat house, and so was this. These are Croat houses. These are also Croat houses (indicating). I've shown you where they are. The photograph is not really a very good one, but I can recognise them.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: By November of 1993, where were the majority of the Muslims living in Rotilj?

utterances.speaker: FATHER IVAN PERVAN
utterances.text: In November 1993, most of the Muslims were living here, here, and over here (indicating).

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: In the far south-eastern corner of the village; would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: FATHER IVAN PERVAN
utterances.text: In the western part of the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Sorry, yes, because the photograph is back to front. Where was most of the damage to the Muslim homes? Where were the houses that were burnt in Rotilj, as far as you can recall?

utterances.speaker: FATHER IVAN PERVAN
utterances.text: Let me just have a look, please. (Indicating).

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Sir, you're pointing on Exhibit 76 to the first Rotilj sticker, which is nearest the main part of Kiseljak. Do you recall how many houses were damaged in that area?

utterances.speaker: FATHER IVAN PERVAN
utterances.text: I said in my testimony yesterday that there were about 15, but I have not counted them to the present day.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: You can take a seat now, Father. Thank you for your help.

utterances.speaker: FATHER IVAN PERVAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, the Court has heard testimony from an UNPROFOR, from a U.N. protection force officer, Captain Lanthier, who visited the village of Rotilj in April and May 1993. He found a community at the far end of the village, as you have indicated, which consisted mostly of women and children and the elderly. Is that your recollection of the conditions in Rotilj in May of '93?

utterances.speaker: FATHER IVAN PERVAN
utterances.text: In May 1993, I went to the house of Salko Hodzic. It was night. Salko greeted me with two other men. The next few days when I went to Rotilj, I usually went to Salko and Suad Betic, and I saw more women and children than men. That was at that period, but I did see men as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Do you know Mr. Mario Bradara?

utterances.speaker: FATHER IVAN PERVAN
utterances.text: Yes. I do know Mario Bradara.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Who is he?

utterances.speaker: FATHER IVAN PERVAN
utterances.text: He is a soldier.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: In the HVO?

utterances.speaker: FATHER IVAN PERVAN
utterances.text: Yes, an HVO soldier.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: In May of 1993, was he an assistant commander of the HVO in Kiseljak?

utterances.speaker: FATHER IVAN PERVAN
utterances.text: I know that he was in the army command, but what particular function he had, I don't know. I never asked him, but I knew he was in the command there.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: The U.N. protection force officer that I just mentioned to you, Captain Lanthier, spoke with Mr. Bradara in May of 1993. Mr. Bradara told him that the Muslims in Rotilj were imprisoned, that they were not free to leave, that the able-bodied men were being used to dig trenches. He also stated that the International Committee for the Red Cross would be denied access to Rotilj. Would you agree with me that that, in fact, was the state of affairs in Rotilj in May of 1993?

utterances.speaker: FATHER IVAN PERVAN
utterances.text: I don't know about this talk that he had. At the time when I was absent, I do not know whether UNPROFOR and the monitors and the Red Cross went to Rotilj. You said that they did go. I still maintain, that is to say, that I commiserate with those people. I know that it was not easy for them. It was very difficult for them. You said that they did go. I don't know whether he prohibited them from doing so, said that they could not. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Those people were not free to leave Rotilj in May of 1993, were they, Mr. Pervan?

utterances.speaker: FATHER IVAN PERVAN
utterances.text: In my testimony, speaking about the roadblock at the entrance to the village of Rotilj, I said that the roadblock was there and that two elderly men stood guard there, manning it. I think that in the psychosis that reigned at the time and in the problems that existed, nobody from Rotilj either wished or had a need to go into the town, because everything was closed. There were exits toward the west in areas. I do not agree that it was a camp, and I would not have justified this, approved of it. Camps are not for people. I know that they had a difficult time, and I know that the roadblock was aimed at, and that's what they told me, stopping anybody doing any harm to the people. Your Honours, let me just add, if I may, the fact that there were people behind the roadblock. I, myself, passed and nobody made any problems for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If the next exhibit could be distributed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: While it's being distributed, Father, this is an ECMM report of the 22nd of May, 1993, so another international organisation in the area. I won't commence reading it until Defence counsel have the document in front of them. The gentlemen manning the barrier, did they have a means of communication with the HVO headquarters in Kiseljak?

utterances.speaker: FATHER IVAN PERVAN
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I didn't hear.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I think you said they had a telephone?

utterances.speaker: FATHER IVAN PERVAN
utterances.text: They had a telephone.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: FATHER IVAN PERVAN
utterances.text: A telephone or the radio station, that is to say, a walkie-talkie.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: This report was written after you had been to Rotilj, and I'll read it to you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Excuse me. This is document 542.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: "The team visited the Muslim community in Rotilj where some 600 Muslims are gathered together in a few houses. The people are not free to move, although this fact is denied by HVO. There is a checkpoint manned by Croat civilians who stop people from Rotilj. Announced crossings by a maximum of two old women are allowed. The people asked for certain specified medicines and plastic to repair broken windows. UNHCR and MDM are informed and will assist soon. Six men are sill missing and expected to be in Kiseljak prison. ICRC will be informed on this matter." Mr. Pervan, are you aware that elderly women had to seek permission to leave Rotilj?

utterances.speaker: FATHER IVAN PERVAN
utterances.text: I am not aware of that, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Were you aware at the time that six men, six Muslim males, from the village, were missing and thought to be in the HVO barracks in Kiseljak?

utterances.speaker: FATHER IVAN PERVAN
utterances.text: No, I was not aware of that then, and I am still not.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Let's move forward in time to September of 1993. Did you visit the village of Rotilj in September?

utterances.speaker: FATHER IVAN PERVAN
utterances.text: I didn't keep notes. I went to the village from time to time. It is quite possible that during that month I was in the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: This is a description of the village given by a Canadian army officer who has testified before these Honourable Judges, and this is a summary of what he stated. He found that there were 600 Muslims living in 15 to 20 houses, and they were mostly women, children and the elderly. They were from, amongst other villages, Visnjice, Dolce, Han Ploca, Duhre and Grahovice; would that accord with your view of conditions in Rotilj in September of 1993?

utterances.speaker: FATHER IVAN PERVAN
utterances.text: I am not aware of it, but if 600 people were mentioned, and you say that they were in 15 to 20 houses, I don't know that at that time there were over 30 individuals in those houses. So, that there were 30 people in each house, I do not know, I was not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, at the time the International Community expressed a deep concern, which the Canadian officer told the Judges about, that winter was coming, and that there was a view that the Muslims of Rotilj were about to undergo extreme suffering and possibly even death during the winter months because of their condition; are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: FATHER IVAN PERVAN
utterances.text: Their fears were not known to me. What I did know was that every house had a wood nearby, which meant enough timber for fires, and that, at that time, they received food, as they did previously, as much as other people received, except what other humanitarian organisations also gave them, and we were not able to control that, nor did we wish to control it, such as the UNHCR, Doctors Without Borders, Chemists Without Borders, UNPROFOR and so on and so forth. This fear at that time that they would undergo extreme suffering, I do not agree with that statement, because other refugees did not have a better or a worse time of it. Perhaps, psychologically, they were stronger than the people who were Muslims, but quite certainly there was enough firewood for fires and food and clothing, just like everybody else who was needy in the parish of Kiseljak, and I do not agree with the statement made by that individual.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: But you didn't live with the Muslims of Rotilj, did you, in the winter months, Father? You were living in your own home.

utterances.speaker: FATHER IVAN PERVAN
utterances.text: Yes, I was living in my own home, and I repeat once more, they were psychologically in an unstable situation. But physically, as regards their physical needs, to drink, to eat, to have clothing and to keep warm, those material needs were satisfied, and they could have even asked for more.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: But you would agree with me that the International Community, Doctors Without Frontiers, UNPROFOR, UNHCR, are a better judge than you of the health and condition of the Muslims in Rotilj in November of 1993?

utterances.speaker: FATHER IVAN PERVAN
utterances.text: I am not a physician and I cannot assess anybody's mental health. I am a man who will give everybody a piece of bread if they come to me and say they are hungry.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Let me distribute the next exhibit, which is a public document.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: The next document, Mr. Pervan, is a public announcement through the French Press Agency by the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees, and I'll read it to you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is 543.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: "Sarajevo, September 25th, 1993. Bosnian Croats have rounded up the Muslim population of several villages in Central Bosnia, using the men as forced labour and locking up women and children in a virtual concentration camp, a UN official said here Saturday. Ray Wilkinson, spokesman for the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees said his fieldworkers had reported that HVO Croat forces had rounded up a significant number of Muslims from the villages around Kiseljak where the UN protection force is based. The men, numbering several hundred, were being used to dig trenches at the front near Fojnica, while women and children had been deported from their homes and taken to the villages of Rotilj, Wilkinson said. International Committee of the Red Cross officials had vainly sought access to the camp, he added." The final paragraph, "News of the deportation comes on the day after Bosnian Croats released over 500 Muslim prisoners from a camp at Dretew in the south of the country, taking them to the island of Korcula off the Croatian coast." Mr. Pervan, this is a public announcement by the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees, you understand that?

utterances.speaker: FATHER IVAN PERVAN
utterances.text: Yes, I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: You would agree with me that they are not an organisation to exaggerate for effect?

utterances.speaker: FATHER IVAN PERVAN
utterances.text: That is probably so.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: You would agree with their description of the conditions in Rotilj in September of 1993?

utterances.speaker: FATHER IVAN PERVAN
utterances.text: They had their view of this, and they presented their view here.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Are you aware that Muslims were rounded up in September from Muslim villages in Kiseljak and taken to Rotilj?

utterances.speaker: FATHER IVAN PERVAN
utterances.text: Muslims from Muslim villages came to Rotilj, but I also know that UNPROFOR would bring them to Rotilj. I also know that UNPROFOR made some kind of exchanges, that they brought Croats from Kacuni, Selac (phoen), and from gaols, and from Brestovsko, and also that some Muslims from Kiseljak, especially from Radanovici, were taken to Rotilj, but also to Muslim territory. I know that at that time UNPROFOR and the monitors did not share the same view about this problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Are you aware that able-bodied men within the village were being used by the HVO for forced trench digging?

utterances.speaker: FATHER IVAN PERVAN
utterances.text: Yes, I'm aware of that. However, I also know that together with them trenches were dug by those Croats who are not fit for combat. They dug those trenches together, at the same time. I know that Muslims from Rotilj would come to the beginning of the village and that they would board trucks there, and then they would be driven away. I know they were given cigarettes and I know that as they would dig trenches they could even drink alcoholic beverages, they could eat, and the trucks would take them back to Rotilj. Croats also dug trenches with them. Elderly men, that is, people from the age of 57 to 70, who could.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: These Muslim males who were digging trenches for the HVO; they were not volunteers, were they, Father?

utterances.speaker: FATHER IVAN PERVAN
utterances.text: Certainly not. I wouldn't do it, either, if I didn't have to.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, the trucks that you mentioned that collected them from the village, these were HVO trucks, were they?

utterances.speaker: FATHER IVAN PERVAN
utterances.text: At that time in Kiseljak we did not have trucks which would be painted in army colours. These were mainly civilian trucks used for army purposes. Until the cease-fire, those trucks were without registration plates or anything, and we would often take trucks to collect food without registration plates, without insurance, without a green card for vehicles. At that time I hardly saw any military trucks in Kiseljak. These were civilian trucks that were used for HVO purposes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, if you wish to take the morning break here, it's a convenient time for me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, we will take a 20-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: The hearing is now resumed. Have the accused brought in, please. (The accused entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Cayley, the floor is yours again to continue with the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. We will continue, Mr. Pervan.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, you said in your examination-in-chief that you met Ivica Rajic almost every other day --

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Nobilo.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would like to suggest that we go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Do you agree, Mr. Cayley?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Of course, for the security of the witness, Mr. President, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Nobilo, we will go into a private session. (Private session)

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: In your examination-in-chief, you stated that you had no recollection of the collection in trucks of the Muslim population from villages in the Kiseljak municipality and the forced movement of those Muslim civilians to Rotilj?

utterances.speaker: FATHER IVAN PERVAN
utterances.text: The problem in Kiseljak was that there were a lot of people there, especially those who had come from other regions. My problem was that 99 per cent of the things that were going on, that were taking place, I got to know of this later on, post-festum. When I learned of these facts, I then reacted to them and stated my views, that is, the views of a man who is a Catholic. According to the lists, in Rotilj, there were more and more people coming in. I did learn of the fact that people, that is to say, Croats were coming from other places, coming in from Bilalovac, for example, most especially, and that some people, Muslims, were taken by UNPROFOR. That was called an exchange at the time. I learned this mostly by people coming to tell me that they had arrived yesterday. They said, "We're here. We arrived yesterday. We need help and we were exchanged." That is when I learned of matters of this kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, the Honourable Judges of this Court have heard evidence from Muslim residents of Han Ploca, of Potkraj, of Duhre, that HVO trucks arrived in those villages and moved the women and children to Rotilj village and the able-bodied men to the Kiseljak barracks. Did you hear about that in 1993 or subsequently?

utterances.speaker: FATHER IVAN PERVAN
utterances.text: I cannot say that these people lied to this Honourable Court. That is certainly the way it was, because in Rotilj, you can check this with the Caritas lists, people who came from Topolj and other places, they lived there. But how each and every one of them got there, that, I really do not know. The state of affairs was as you say. That is to say, they came from other places to Rotilj. I do not know when, how, and at what time they came, and I cannot say that these people are lying. This may be the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Father. You've been very frank with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: We will now move on to another area of inquiry, and if I can ask that we now move back into private session, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, private session, please. (Private session)

utterances.text: What is the number of this exhibit, Mr. Dubuisson?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
